Extending the Martian landslide inventory southward: distribution, landslide types, and latitudinal extent
papers.summary: Martian landslide inventories remain concentrated near the equator, particularly in Valles Marineris. We present 411 previously uncatalogued landslides spanning 63°S–34°N, extending coverage of the southern mid-latitudes and increasing the existing global catalogue by approximately 13%. Most events (73.7%) occur between 20°S and 50°S, and 84.9% originate within Early and Middle Noachian highland units. Rock avalanches dominate (49.1%), followed by slumps (26.8%), rock avalanche/ejecta forms (12.2%), and slump/rock avalanche transitions (11.9%). The apparent mobility index (H/L) ranges from 0.03 to 0.31 (5th–95th percentiles) and generally decreases with landslide area, although this relationship varies by type. No significant inventory-wide relationship exists between mobility and latitude. Crater size–frequency distributions of selected deposits indicate predominantly Late Amazonian model surface ages, with older surfaces reaching 1.68 ± 0.48 Ga. This inventory provides new spatial, morphological, and chronological constraints on mass wasting beyond the well-studied canyon systems.

papers.title: Landslide susceptibility assessment in Le'an County using machine learning approaches
papers.source: International Conference on Remote Sensing, Mapping, and Geographic Information Systems (RSMG)
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility assessment is a core pre-step in geological disaster risk Landslide susceptibility assessment is a core pre-step in geological disaster risk prevention and control. Traditional assessment methods have significant limitations in verifying the precision gain effect of factor screening and quantifying the influence of multicollinearity among multiple factors. This paper takes Le'an County in Jiangxi Province, a typical landslide-prone county in the southern red soil hilly area, as the research area. Based on a 12.5 m DEM, the research area is divided into 50,522 slope units, and a disaster-prone factor table including 15 core factors such as elevation, slope, and NDVI is constructed, forming a refined landslide susceptibility evaluation system based on slope units. Using the dual diagnostic method of Pearson correlation coefficient and variance inflation factor (VIF), 10 core evaluation factors without significant collinearity were identified. Model training and performance assessment were implemented based on the selected dataset through spatial 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that after eliminating redundant factors, the accuracy of each model has significantly improved. Specifically, the RF model outperformed the other counterparts, attaining a training accuracy of 0.824, a validation accuracy of 0.817, and an AUC of 0.84. These results markedly outperformed those of the LR model (AUC=0.74) and the SVM model (AUC=0.76). The areas with extremely high susceptibility to landslides are concentrated in the southeastern part of Le'an County, which is highly consistent with the coupled driving mechanism of topography, hydrology and soil.

papers.title: Investigation of Potentially Hazardous Landslides Using Geolectric Resistivity Methods and Internal Friction Angle in The Sentool Plantation, Panti-Jember
papers.source: Lambda Jurnal Ilmiah Pendidikan MIPA dan Aplikasinya
papers.summary: The Sentool plantation is situated on the slopes of Mt. Argopuro in Suci Village, Panti District, Jember Regency. This area, previously abandoned, has been transformed into a thriving coffee plantation. Flash floods and landslides in Panti District in 2006 and landslides in the Sentool Plantation in 2015 prompted a study of the subsurface structure, particularly concerning soil types and their stability towards landslide potency. This study combines in situ method using geoelectric resistivity and laboratory tests, including plasticity index (PI) and soil gradation tests. Geoelectric resistivity data acquisition was conducted on two lines using a Wenner-Schlumberger array, with a length of 150 m and a spacing of 5 m. Soil samples were taken at Line 2, namely at a distance of 40 m as sample 1 and 120 m as sample 2. Field research results using the Wenner-Schlumberger array of geoelectric resistivity method on Lines 1 and 2 in the Sentool Plantation show that the subsurface structure is dominated by silty clay and silty soils with resistivity (11.8 – 93.4) ?m and there are several intercalations of sand, gravel, or bedrock with higher resistivity. The plasticity index test results for sample 1 with a PI of 10.45% and sample 2 with a PI of 13.68% show that the soil layers are composed of silty clay silt with moderate plastic. The soil gradation analysis results also indicate that both soil samples are fine-grained (possibly silt) with grain sizes <0.075 mm. Both laboratory test results validate the geoelectric resistivity field research results, which show the dominance of clay soil with a reference internal friction angle (?) of 25° - 30°. The Sentool Plantation research area is characterized by silty clay soils, which may influence subsurface conditions relevant to landslide vulnerability.

papers.title: Climatology and trends of observed daily and hourly extreme precipitation in the French Alps
papers.summary: Abstract. The French Alps are characterized by complex topography, which influences precipitation regimes and associated risks in various ways. Extreme precipitation, especially when it happens on very short timescales, can lead to flash floods and landslides with important social and economic impacts. Local stakeholders, working on prevention and protection from such events, report a perceived recent increase in sub-daily extreme precipitation intensities in the French Alps. However, to our knowledge, this has not yet been confirmed statistically. In this paper, we apply a statistical approach based on extreme value theory on long time series of in situ observations. By comparing daily and hourly observations and analysing both months and seasons, we are able to present a climatology as well as trends of precipitation extremes in unprecedented detail. Here we define 'extreme' as 20-year return levels of precipitation intensity, focusing thus on very rare events. In a first part, we use a stationary framework to provide an updated climatology of daily and hourly extremes. We make use of an existing weather pattern classification to show the dynamic influences on precipitation maxima, highlighting the strong differences between the northern and the southern French Alps as well as between seasons. In a second part, we compute trends of these extremes, for which we also find partially large differences between regions and seasons. For annual extremes of daily precipitation, we find strong positive trends in the south and negative trends in the north, mostly driven by changes in autumn. Annual trends of hourly extremes are mostly non-significant and show more of an east-west division, with positive trends in the high Alps and negative ones in the pre-Alps.

papers.title: Tsunamigenic potential of flank instabilities of Kameni Volcano inside Santorini Caldera, southern Aegean
papers.summary: Located in the southern Aegean Sea, the Santorini volcanic complex represents one of the most geodynamically active and hazardous volcano–tectonic systems in the Mediterranean. Following the Late Bronze Age caldera-forming eruption (~ 1600 BCE ), the Kameni volcanic edifice emerged within the central caldera. On the northwestern flank of Nea Kameni, lava flows are superposed on unconsolidated pyroclastic deposits, primarily pumice and ash attributed to the 726 CE submarine explosive eruption. These units reside on a topographic step coincident with a major volcano–tectonic lineament, a geomorphological configuration that exhibits structural parallels to the pre−2018 sector collapse state of Anak Krakatau. Here, we employ the Landslide-HySEA numerical code to simulate tsunami generation and propagation resulting from various potential flank instability scenarios of Nea Kameni. Three distinct collapse volumes were modeled: 0.057 km 3 , 0.077 km 3 , and 0.13 km 3 . The simulations demonstrate substantial hazardous potential; a flank failure of 0.13 km 3 has the potential to generate maximum coastal wave amplitudes of up to 39 m. Furthermore, all modeled scenarios result in tsunami heights exceeding 2 m at multiple critical coastal locations. These results indicate that such events would inflict severe damage on critical infrastructure and high-density maritime hubs situated along the inner caldera cliffs. Seafloor microbathymetry acquired through a photogrammetric tow-sled system suggests little remobilization despite ongoing volcano–seismic activity. Yet, our findings underscore the necessity for continuous monitoring of the structural stability of the Kameni volcanic edifice and emphasize the requirement to integrate flank-collapse mechanisms into the tsunami hazard assessment frameworks for Santorini.

papers.title: An Optimized Method for Slope Deformation Monitoring via Parallel-Track InSAR Data Fusion
papers.summary: Abstract. This study addresses geometric distortion in SAR imagery caused by complex topography in reservoir areas, which adversely affects the accuracy of InSAR monitoring. A multi-orbit data fusion technique is proposed, integrating the R-Index(im) with an improved Geometric Distortion (GD) Index. Using the study landslide mass at Danjiangkou Reservoir as a case study, the research leverages Sentinel-1A satellite data. The GD index model is optimized by incorporating a shadow effect coefficient (Sh). Combined with the R-Index(im) 's capability for distortion-region identification, an adaptive weighted fusion model is established. Empirical analysis demonstrates that this approach effectively corrects deformation monitoring biases caused by geometric distortion. Compared to single-orbit data, the fusion results reduce deformation rate errors by 0.02 mm/year and 0.36 mm/year, while expanding the monitoring coverage by 32 %. Verification against GNSS ground-truth data confirms that this method significantly enhances the accuracy and reliability of InSAR monitoring in complex terrain, offering an effective technical solution for reservoir landslide early warning.

papers.title: Hydro-mechanical assessment of tunnel–fill slope systems under extreme rainfall: effects of foundations and slope protection
papers.summary: Tunnel excavation through fill slopes under extreme rainfall involves complex hydro-mechanical interactions among excavation-induced stress redistribution, rainfall infiltration, slope deformation, and adjacent infrastructure. This study investigates the response and stability of a tunnel–fill slope system using integrated physical model testing and numerical simulation. The physical experiments examined rainfall infiltration, ground settlement, stress redistribution, and pore-water-pressure evolution during excavation. The validation test simulated an upper-range heavy-rainfall event of 200 mm/day for 12 h at prototype scale, corresponding to approximately 16.67 mm/day applied for 1 h in the 1:120-scale model. Agreement between the experimental and numerical results confirmed the model’s ability to reproduce the principal hydraulic and deformation responses. Two parametric investigations were subsequently conducted. The first evaluated the effects of adjacent buildings and foundation systems under rainfall and dry conditions, focusing on building settlement and slope-supporting pile displacement. The second assessed riprap, geocell reinforcement, and vegetation under rainfall without building loads by examining slope deformation and pore-water-pressure development. The results demonstrate that rainfall intensifies hydro-mechanical responses and structural deformation, while the effectiveness of protection measures varies according to their hydraulic and mechanical functions. These findings support the selection of suitable foundation systems and slope-protection strategies in complex urban fill-slope environments.

papers.title: Simulation-Informed Machine Learning for Multiclass Landslide and Debris-Flow Hazard Classification in a Recently Urbanized City, Republic of Korea
papers.summary: Rapid urban expansion into mountainous terrain, together with increasing exposure to extreme weather, has increased the need for transparent and interpretable slope-hazard assessment in forested and residential mountain environments. However, relatively few studies have integrated field-survey information with physically based simulation outputs for interpretable multi-class classification within an established slope-hazard grading framework. This pilot study developed a simulation-informed machine-learning framework for classifying composite slope-hazard grades (Grades I–III) using 71 landslide-prone and 52 debris-flow-prone sites in Sejong City, Republic of Korea. For the landslide dataset, selected field-survey indicators were integrated with SoilWorks-derived slope-stability information, whereas for the debris-flow dataset, selected field-survey indicators were integrated with FLO-2D-derived simulation information. Four machine-learning algorithms—Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM)—were evaluated under severe class imbalance. RF showed the strongest overall performance in the original holdout evaluation, achieving an accuracy of 0.857 for both datasets and weighted F1-scores of 0.849 for the landslide dataset and 0.836 for the debris-flow dataset. Gini importance, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), and targeted ablation analysis indicated that simulation-derived variables provided strong discriminatory information within the established grading framework. papers.summary: Abstract. Ground motion poses a significant threat to the safety and functionality of transport infrastructure, particularly in regions affected by landslides, subsidence, freeze–thaw processes, and large-scale tunnelling. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) enables millimeter-level displacement monitoring over large areas and is used to support infrastructure risk assessment. Here, we evaluate the usability of two InSAR approaches, (i) Persistent Scatterer Interferometry (PSI) using displacement products from the European Ground Motion Service (EGMS), and (ii) a combined Persistent- and Distributed-Scatterer (PS+DS) phase-linking workflow across key Swedish transport corridors. Rather than a strictly controlled methodological comparison, we evaluate how differences between operational InSAR solutions translate into practical performance for infrastructure monitoring. Results show that PS+DS consistently yields five times as many measurement points while maintaining RMSE values within a similar range to EGMS (mostly below 6 mm in the Line Of Sight direction). The EGMS exhibits narrower RMSE distributions, but PS+DS achieves comparable median RMSE of the measurement points across most land-cover types and corridor environments. Both datasets capture similar displacement patterns along all corridors, with measurement points from both approaches concentrating within the linear corridor geometry. Overall, the five-fold increase in PS+DS point density offers infrastructure operators a practical pathway to finer-scale ground motion monitoring for railway maintenance and risk assessment, while demonstrating how the choice of operational InSAR processing strategy shapes the information available for Earth-observation-based infrastructure applications.

papers.title: Potential erosion risk assessment of Kanak stream basin (Sivas, Sarkisla) with the ICONA model
papers.source: Frontiers in Life Sciences and Related Technologies
papers.summary: The rapid development of technology following the Industrial Revolution has increased human domination over nature. Erosion, which plays a critical role in the process of natural shaping of the earth, can accelerate over time because of improper utilization of the natural environment by humans. The main objective of this study is to determine the erosion susceptibility of the Kanak Creek Basin, one of the sub-basins in the upper reaches of the Kizilirmak River, using the ICONA model, whose main parameters are slope, lithology, land use and vegetation cover, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Remote Sensing techniques, and to list the measures that can be taken against erosion. According to the results of the ICONA model potential erosion level map, 48% of the study area has low erosion susceptibility. These areas largely correspond to the vicinity of Sama Mountain, which has volcanic rocks resistant to erosion, and the base of Sarkisla Plain where the slope is very low. The plain floor is largely covered with agricultural lands. The expansion of irrigated agriculture in this region is one of the main measures that can be taken against erosion. Erosion susceptibility increases around Turna Mountain on the northern border of the basin and Cal Mountain in the south due to both the increase in slope and the lack of resistance of the rocks in the region to erosion, and corresponds to 30% of the study area. In 22% of the basin, susceptibility to erosion is at a medium level. Most of these areas consist of natural meadows and pastures. It is essential to take measures against overgrazing in these areas to prevent the complete loss of the already sparse vegetation cover. Planning land use in the basin in a sustainable manner, arranging fields and layers perpendicular to the slope, expanding irrigated agriculture, and preventing overgrazing are of vital importance in terms of combating soil erosion.

papers.title: Effects of waveguide tube geometry and surrounding medium conditions on acoustic emission signal attenuation
papers.summary: Deep-seated deformation in landslides is typically concealed and exhibits a time lag; reliably obtaining information on internal deformation through acoustic emission (AE) technology remains a key challenge in landslide early warning. Metal waveguides can reduce the impact of strong soil attenuation on AE signal acquisition; however, the mechanisms of propagation attenuation within the metal waveguides themselves remain unclear. To address this, this study conducted controlled laboratory experiments on wave propagation in waveguide tubes to systematically investigate the differences in propagation attenuation caused by waveguide diameter, wall thickness, and the state of the surrounding medium. By analyzing time-domain waveforms, frequency-domain characteristics, time–frequency representations, and fitting exponential attenuation models, the study examined the attenuation changes with increasing propagation distance under different operating conditions. The results indicate that the amplitude of AE signals generally exhibits exponential attenuation as the propagation distance increases. When comparing individual factors, the surrounding-medium condition produced the largest change in attenuation, followed by outer diameter, whereas wall thickness had the weakest effect. Attenuation was also frequency selective. These findings provide a basis for selecting components for active waveguide systems (AWS), determining sensor spacing, and establishing effective monitoring ranges.

papers.title: Weather and Landslide Data Analysis Using Spatio-Temporal and Categorical Data Mining
papers.summary: This paper proposes a semantic correlation and knowledge mining method that identifies semantic correlation structures between two sets with different granularities and numbers of elements, and performs semantic interpretation and knowledge representation of coarse-grained events. When humans understand an event, we do not refer only to a single element that directly corresponds to the event. Instead, use the time before and after the event, the space in which the event occurred, and related concepts as clues. We then select semantically related subsets from a large amount of surrounding information and integrate them as the background of the event. The proposed method aims to computationally formalize this process of background exploration. The proposed method targets a set $A$, which contains many fine-grained elements, and a set $B$, which contains a small number of coarse-grained elements. For each $b_j \in B$, the method constructs a semantically related subset $A_j \subseteq A$ from set $A$. Each element is represented in a semantic space $S$ composed of time, space, and vocabulary, and the semantic correlation between the aggregated representation of the subset and the representation of $b_j$ is computed. Through this process, the proposed method explicitly describes latent correspondences between data sets with different granularities and representation formats as subset-level correlation structures, and provides a framework for transforming these structures into reusable knowledge representations. Furthermore, this paper applies the proposed method to the disaster prevention domain and demonstrates that semantic correlation structures can be constructed between meteorological observation data and landslide event data. The results confirm that the proposed method is effective for the integrated understanding of heterogeneous data sets and for knowledge extraction.

papers.summary: Slope stability prediction is a critical challenge in geotechnical engineering. This challenge arises from the complex nonlinear interactions among multiple influencing factors such as soil properties, slope geometry, and hydraulic conditions. Traditional analytical methods rely on simplified assumptions that fail to capture these complex relationships. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid predictive framework that integrates machine learning models with intelligent optimization algorithms. Six key parameters, including unit weight, cohesion, internal friction angle, slope angle, slope height, and pore water pressure ratio, are selected as input features. Three machine learning models, namely Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Machine, are optimized using four intelligent optimization algorithms, including the Sparrow Search Algorithm, Lion Swarm Optimization, Whale Optimization Algorithm, and Genetic Algorithm, resulting in twelve combined configurations. Validation using ten independent engineering cases confirms that the predictions of this model are consistent with actual slope conditions, demonstrating strong engineering applicability. This study provides a systematic comparative framework for hybrid model selection and offers practical guidance for intelligent slope stability assessment.

papers.summary: ABSTRACT Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are increasingly recognized as sustainable approaches for addressing water insecurity, land degradation, biodiversity loss, and climate resilience. However, robust long-term field evidence quantifying their hydrological and ecological effectiveness remains limited. This study presents a multi-decadal (1985–2025) evidence synthesis evaluating bamboo-based NbS for restoring degraded ravine landscapes in India by integrating long-term field observations, experimental watershed investigations, hydrological monitoring, project datasets, and peer-reviewed literature. Results demonstrate that bamboo functions as living hydrological infrastructure by enhancing rainfall retention, increasing infiltration, reducing runoff and sediment transport, improving soil quality, and accelerating ecological recovery. Bamboo-based interventions reduced runoff by 80–90%, soil loss by 85–95%, and sediment yield by over 90%, while stabilizing gullies within 2–3 years. Infiltration increased substantially (up to ∼140 cm h−1) together with improvements in soil organic carbon and micro-ecological conditions. Economically, bamboo systems generated annual returns of ₹33,500–48,000 ha−1 with internal rates of return of 18–22%. The study proposes an integrated Nature-Based Hydrological Engineering framework, establishing bamboo as a scalable, climate-resilient solution for watershed restoration, erosion control, and sustainable water management in degraded landscapes worldwide.

papers.summary: Jeju Island relies heavily on groundwater recharged through its permeable volcanic terrain. This study examines how development of the Jeju Global Education City, where site construction began in 2009, changed surface infiltration and what this implies for groundwater recharge. Land-cover maps from 2007 and 2025 were compared over 378.9 ha of mapped cover within the legal planning boundary. Single-ring infiltration tests were carried out on Gotjawal, rough grass and artificial grass, with five trials per surface; one rough-grass trial did not finish within 300 s and was excluded from rate statistics. Under a scenario that treats artificial grass as non-recharging, the share of the site treated as sealed rose from 2.5% to 27.8%, an increase of approximately 95.9 ha. Every Gotjawal trial infiltrated faster than every grass trial, although the apparatus supports only a relative comparison. Applying published recharge fractions of 9 to 48% to rainfall on the newly sealed area gives a potential recharge loss of 102,000 to 545,000 m³ per year from sealing alone. These are conditional estimates rather than a measured change in aquifer recharge.

papers.title: Biodegradable mulch films affecting surface runoff, soil erosion, and film fragment loss from farmland
papers.summary: The use of conventional plastic mulch films is a common agricultural practice that can lead to persistent plastic film fragments entering soil systems. To prevent the accumulation of these fragments, soil-biodegradable mulch films are marketed as alternatives. Unlike conventional plastic mulch, soil-biodegradable mulch films are ploughed into the soil after use, where they biodegrade over time. This study aims to elucidate the effects of soil-biodegradable mulch film fragments—following six months of application on the soil surface—ploughed into soil on surface runoff, soil erosion, and lateral mulch film fragment loss during simulated rainfall events. Our results showed a significant increase in runoff coefficient for the pre-wetted (wet run) simulations in soils with soil-biodegradable mulch film fragments compared to soils without them, while differences in sediment delivery were insignificant. In the delivered sediments, large mulch film fragments (> 2 mm) were depleted, whereas small fragments (< 2 mm) were transported approximately proportionally to the topsoil of the plots. Overall, our results indicate that film fragments can affect surface runoff on arable land, and generally, soil erosion is a pathway of soil-biodegradable mulch film fragments transport into adjacent ecosystems, which is especially effective in the case of small film fragments (< 2 mm) available from topsoil.

papers.source: Scholarly Journal of Science and Technology Research and Development
papers.summary: Spatial variability in soil properties strongly influences water dynamics, nutrient availability, and crop productivity in tropical agroecosystems, thereby affecting the sustainability of climate-smart rice production systems. This study evaluated the spatial variability of selected soil physical, hydraulic, and chemical properties across four agro-ecological zones (Awka, Anambra, Aguata, and Onitsha) of Anambra State, southeastern Nigeria. Surface soil samples (0–30 cm) were collected from georeferenced locations differing in elevation and landscape characteristics. Laboratory analyses were conducted to determine particle size distribution, bulk density (BD), saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat), soil pH, and organic matter (OM). Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), correlation analysis, and principal component analysis (PCA) were employed to evaluate variability and relationships among soil properties. Results revealed considerable spatial heterogeneity across the study area. Sand content ranged from 332 to 582 g kg⁻¹, while clay content varied between 218 and 354 g kg⁻¹. Bulk density ranged from 1.346 to 1.458 g cm⁻³, whereas Ksat varied from 0.0182 to 0.0468 cm hr⁻¹. Soil pH was moderately acidic (5.3–5.7), while OM content ranged from 2.2 to 3.3%. ANOVA indicated no significant zonal differences in Ksat and BD, suggesting that micro-scale variability exerted a stronger influence than agro-ecological classification. PCA explained 96.5% of total variability, with soil texture and hydraulic properties constituting the dominant controlling factors. The findings highlight the importance of site-specific soil and water management strategies for improving rice productivity, enhancing water-use efficiency, and strengthening climate resilience in southeastern Nigeria.

Physico-chemical and chemical analyses were carried out on the groundwater to characterise the distribution of several elements associated with mining activities, notably copper (Cu), cadmium (Cd), cyanide (CN⁻), arsenic (As), lead (Pb) and mercury (Hg). The data were analysed using statistical methods, notably Wilk’s alpha test and ANOVA. Intrinsic vulnerability was assessed using the PaPRI approach, based on the criteria of Protection, Reservoir and Infiltration. The results show spatial variability in the chemical quality of groundwater. Cu, Cd, CN⁻ and As generally exhibit low concentrations and low spatial variability, whilst Pb and Hg show significant variations between sampling points. The vulnerability assessment indicates that 80 per cent of the area is highly vulnerable and 10 per cent is extremely vulnerable, meaning that 90 per cent of the area is characterised as being highly or extremely vulnerable. This situation reflects the aquifer’s significant susceptibility to potential contaminant transfer from the surface. The combination of hydrochemical data and PaPRI mapping therefore provides a useful tool for identifying priority monitoring areas and contributing to the sustainable protection of groundwater resources in the Angovia mining area.

papers.summary: Water-Absorbing Roads as Sustainable Urban Drainage Infrastructure This project focuses on the concept of water-absorbing roads, technically known as permeable pavement systems. These roads are designed to allow rainwater to pass through a porous surface or permeable joints into the underlying layers, where it is temporarily stored in an aggregate reservoir before infiltrating into the soil or being discharged through an underdrain. The project explores different types of permeable pavements, including porous asphalt, pervious concrete, and permeable interlocking concrete pavement. It explains the functions of pavement layers, water infiltration, drainage arrangements, construction materials, and maintenance requirements. The main objective of this project is to study how permeable pavement systems can help reduce surface runoff, minimise waterlogging, and support sustainable stormwater management, particularly in urban areas experiencing heavy monsoon rainfall. The project also examines the limitations of these systems, including clogging, soil permeability, groundwater conditions, and traffic loads. This is a conceptual, literature-supported study that highlights the importance of proper site investigation, engineering design, and regular maintenance. It presents permeable roads as a potential supplement to conventional drainage systems for developing more sustainable and resilient road infrastructure.

In contrast, GUA alone resulted in the lowest compressive strength and mass flux rates. These findings suggest that combining cyanobacteria with OSCPs, particularly CMC, is an effective strategy for promoting biocrust formation and mitigating soil erosion in arid environments.

papers.title: Synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation on microplastic and nanoplastic removal from stormwater runoff in bioretention systems
papers.summary: Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) are emerging contaminants in stormwater runoff, posing potential ecological and human health risks. Bioretention systems offer promising nature-based stormwater treatment, yet their performance remains highly variable. Biochar, particularly post-processed biochar, has demonstrated strong potential for contaminant removal; however, its effects on MNP removal, leachate quality, and plant performance in green infrastructure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the combined effects of untreated and thermal air-oxidated (hereinafter: treated) biochars and native vegetation ( Rudbeckia hirta ) on the removal of polystyrene MNPs (0.02, 0.2, and 1 μm) from synthetic stormwater runoff, leachate quality and plant performance in bioretention systems. Both biochars effectively removed nanoplastics during the early MNP-spiked storm events. Vegetation substantially reduced MNP leaching during subsequent simulated rainfall events, supported by the detection of microplastics within root tissues, indicating plant uptake. Vegetation also reduced nutrient leaching, with larger plants exhibiting more pronounced effects, highlighting the importance of enhancing plant growth for contaminant removal. Although treated biochar reduced total organic carbon leaching during initial spiking events, both biochars increased P, K, and S leaching. Overall, our findings demonstrate synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation in enhancing contaminant retention in bioretention systems, advancing green infrastructure design and sustainable stormwater management.

We investigated groundwater-surface-water connectivity and groundwater age distributions in the Santa Elena Ophiolite (SEO), Costa Rica, where strongly monsoonal recharge provides a natural setting for resolving fluid circulation through ultramafic terrain. Groundwater, surface water, and hyperalkaline springs were characterized using tritium ( 3 H), stable water isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H), discharge, infiltration, and wet/dry stream surveys. Tritium ranged from 0.06 to 0.85 TU, compared with a 2015-2022 Costa Rican precipitation mean of 1.17 ± 0.20 TU. Surface waters contained 0.53-0.85 TU, consistent with an apparent age of ~8 years, whereas hyperalkaline springs under baseflow conditions contained only 0.06-0.09 TU, indicating apparent groundwater ages >60 years. Stable water isotopes further reveal connectivity among precipitation, shallow groundwater, and deeper hyperalkaline circulation. Moderate stream alkalinity (pH 8-9) and substantial streambed degassing further suggest diffuse deep-groundwater inputs across SEO’s CZ. papers.title: Integrating land resource inventory and hydrology to transform rainfed agriculture towards sustainable intensification
papers.summary: Context Rainfed agriculture in semi-arid regions is constrained not only by rainfall scarcity but also by inefficient conversion of rainfall into plant-available water. Large yield gaps persist because of poor rainfall partitioning, limited soil-moisture storage, and weak integration of land, water, and cropping-system management. Objective This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated Land Resource Inventory (LRI)–hydrology framework for improving water availability and guiding sustainable cropping-system intensification in semi-arid rainfed systems. Methods The framework was developed using long-term experimental evidence from ICRISAT's heritage watersheds in Alfisols and Vertisols, integrating soil–water characterization, rainfall–runoff relationships, landform management, and water budgeting. It was subsequently applied in Bundelkhand, central India, across a ~ 5000-ha geographical landscape (~3000 ha agricultural land), using LRI-based planning, hydrological analysis, and targeted natural resource management interventions. papers.title: Application of the Natural Resources Conservation Service Technical Release 55 Method in Stormwater Management for Land Development Projects: A Practitioner Case Study
papers.summary: The Natural Resources Conservation Service Technical Release 55 (TR-55) method remains one of the most widely used tools for estimating runoff on small land development sites in the United States, and in many Pennsylvania municipalities it is effectively the default method required for stormwater submissions. Most published work on the method concerns its theoretical basis, particularly the curve number and the initial abstraction ratio, while comparatively little describes how practicing engineers actually apply it and defend it in review. This paper documents that practice from the perspective of a civil engineer preparing site design and stormwater management plans for land development projects in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. It describes when the runoff calculation takes place in a typical project, how the principal inputs are selected (curve number from mapped hydrologic soil groups, time of concentration from segmented flow paths with a 100-foot sheet-flow limit, and rainfall depths from NOAA Atlas 14 checked against municipal ordinances), and how pre-development conditions are established on previously disturbed sites. These choices are then illustrated through one example from current practice: a townhouse development of approximately 3.5 acres, where the calculations led to two infiltration basins and a vegetated swale. The example shows how the hydrologic result meets the ordinance requirement, while site geometry, groundwater, infiltration rates, easements, utilities, and cost determine the final facility design. papers.title: Morphometric analysis and prioritization of Virupapura micro-watersheds using GIS and remote sensing techniques in Cauvery River Basin, India
papers.summary: Abstract Morphometric analysis is important for understanding watershed behaviour and supporting sustainable resource management, especially under changing climate and water stress conditions. This study evaluates morphometric characteristics and prioritizes eight micro-watersheds in the Virupapura sub-watershed, Cauvery River Basin, Karnataka, using GIS and remote sensing techniques. Watershed delineation, drainage extraction and parameter calculations were carried out using a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) in ArcGIS 10.8, and stream ordering was performed using the Arthur Strahler [66] method. The watershed is a fifth-order basin with a well-developed drainage network consisting of 119 first-order streams and a high bifurcation ratio (7.75–9.50), indicating structural control. Moderate drainage density (2.164 km/km 2 ) and stream frequency (2.74) suggest balanced runoff and infiltration, while the elongated basin shape and gentle slope reduce erosion risk. Hypsometric analysis showed integral values ranging from 0.151 to 0.484, indicating that the micro-watersheds are in mature to old geomorphic stages with varying levels of erosion susceptibility. Based on prioritization ranking using compound factor (Cf) values, Dholenahalli (Rank 1; Cf = 3.1) was identified as the most critical micro-watershed requiring immediate conservation measures, followed by Chikkamaskallu (Rank 2; Cf = 3.6) and K.G. Mallappanahalli (Rank 3; Cf = 3.9). These results are consistent with recent studies in semi-arid regions reporting increasing watershed degradation under climate variability and anthropogenic pressure. Given present challenges such as groundwater depletion, irregular rainfall and land degradation, the study highlights the need for targeted soil and water conservation measures, rainwater harvesting structures and scientific watershed planning for long-term sustainability.

papers.title: Analisis Multi-Kriteria Wilayah Potensi Air Tanah Menggunakan Analytical Hierarchy Proccess (AHP) dan GIS di Kabupaten Timor Tengah Utara
papers.summary: Groundwater availability is a critical issue in North Central Timor (TTU) Regency, a semi-arid region characterized by seasonal rainfall and limited surface water resources. This study aimed to map groundwater potential using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Four main parameters were analyzed, namely hydrogeology, rainfall, topography, and land cover. The AHP method was applied to determine the weight of each parameter, while GIS was used for spatial analysis and thematic map overlay. The weighting results indicate that hydrogeology is the most influential parameter with a weight of 55%, followed by rainfall (25%), topography (12%), and land cover (8%). The spatial analysis produced five groundwater potential classes: very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. Areas with high to very high groundwater potential are mainly distributed in the southern part of TTU, including Noemuti, Noemuti Timur, Bikomi Selatan, Miomaffo Barat, Insana, sebagian Mutis, dan Biboki Anleu, which are supported by productive aquifers and favorable infiltration conditions. The study demonstrates that the integration of AHP and GIS is effective as a decision-support tool for groundwater exploration and sustainable water resource management in semi-arid regions.

papers.source: Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment
papers.summary: Abstract Uncertainties of hydraulic parameters in representing land-surface characteristics of revegetating riparian zones remains a critical limitation in hydrodynamic flood modelling, particularly when riparian revegetation is implemented as a nature-based solution (NbS) for downstream flood mitigation. This study presents an integrated and systematic framework for uncertainty and sensitivity analysis to evaluate the effectiveness of riparian revegetation in reducing downstream flood hazard, demonstrated in the Bundamba Creek sub-catchment, Australia. The framework combines efficient parameter space exploration using multiple sampling techniques, rain-on-grid hydrodynamic modelling, and an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) surrogate model. Key hydraulic parameters, particularly Manning’s roughness associated with vegetation, are analysed within a realistic range of n = 0.07–0.26, representing sparse grass to dense riparian vegetation. An optimal sampling strategy is selected to ensure both global coverage and concentration within the most probable range of roughness ( n ≈ 0.10–0.20). The ANFIS model demonstrates strong predictive performance (NSE = 0.94; RMSE= 564 m 2 ), enabling rapid evaluation of a large number of scenarios. Results reveal that the most significant reduction in downstream high-hazard area occurs within critical roughness intervals ( n ≈ 0.13–0.16 and 0.22–0.24), where small increases in roughness lead to disproportionately large decreases in hazard extent. Sensitivity peaks at AEP = 1%, indicating that NbS effectiveness is maximized under moderate flood conditions, while the influence diminishes for extreme events. A hierarchical calibration strategy was applied to reproduce overland flow generation, flow velocities in sheet and rill domains and sediment detachment sequentially, allowing the dominant controls on HOF and erosion processes to be identified. Consequently, downslope kinetic energy transport became increasingly dominant within the rill domain, while the overall system remained friction dominated. papers.title: Assessment of Soil and Groundwater Contamination Around an MSW Disposal Site in Jaipur, India
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Despite leachate contamination being common around dumpsites, studies integrating spatial variation, soil‐depth profiles, groundwater quality, and associated environmental risks remain limited. This study assessed leachate, soil, and groundwater quality in the vicinity of a municipal solid‐waste dumpsite in Jaipur, India, using spatial sampling structured by distance, direction, and soil depth. Leachate was alkaline and reducing, with pH of 8.2–8.8, electrical conductivity (EC) of 25–29 mS cm −1 , total dissolved solids (TDS) of 12,460–16,000 mg L −1 , and detectable Cd, Cr, Cu, Pb, Ni, and Zn. Maximum soil EC and TDS values were higher at 0.3 m, whereas selected water‐extractable ions showed variable depth profiles. Groundwater pH ranged from 6.5 to 8.2, EC from 0.4 to 3.6 mS cm −1 , and TDS from 200 to 1770 mg L −1 . Borewells east of the study dumpsite showed the highest EC, TDS, and chloride concentrations. Spearman analysis showed depth‐specific soil associations and groundwater EC‐TDS‐chloride‐calcium co‐variation. Ecological‐risk assessment identified Cd as the principal soil‐risk driver, with moderate to considerable integrated ecological risk across the investigated soil profile. Soil non‐carcinogenic hazard indices were below 1 for adults and children, whereas groundwater‐ingestion hazard indices exceeded 1 at assessed locations, particularly for children, and were dominated by Cd. The absence of a consistent concentration decline with distance or depth indicates heterogeneous spatial and vertical variation. The single‐campaign spatial design did not confirm source attribution or transport pathways. Leachate treatment, runoff control, protection of groundwater‐use areas, and seasonal monitoring are recommended.

papers.title: Why unsaturated soil mechanics matters in Forensic Investigation
papers.summary: Forensic investigation of civil engineering failures has traditionally been conducted within the framework of saturated soil mechanics. However, many natural and engineered ground systems exist in a partially saturated state, where the mechanical response is governed not only by effective stress but also by matric suction and its evolution. This is particularly relevant in environments such as Australia, where soils are frequently unsaturated. This paper highlights the critical role of unsaturated soil mechanics in improving the accuracy and reliability of forensic assessments of geotechnical and structural failures. Key mechanisms associated with unsaturated conditions are examined, including suction-induced apparent cohesion, collapse upon wetting, and shrink–swell behaviour. These processes can lead to significant temporal variations in shear strength, stiffness, and volume, often without any change in external loading. As a result, failures may be triggered by environmental factors such as rainfall infiltration, leakage, or seasonal moisture fluctuations, rather than by structural inadequacy alone. The paper emphasises the importance of the soil–water characteristic curve (SWCC) in linking hydraulic and mechanical behaviour, enabling reconstruction of pre- and post-failure conditions. Typical soil properties requirements in forensic assessments are discussed, including the variation of soil characteristics with changes in moisture condition, slope instability following intense rainfall, differential settlement of shallow foundations due to wetting-induced collapse, and damage to pavements and lightly loaded structures in expansive soils. The limitations of conventional saturated analyses are demonstrated, and the need to incorporate unsaturated constitutive models together with field measurements of suction and moisture content is highlighted. papers.title: Good, Bad and Ugly: Success and failure managing two colluvial landslides in NSW
papers.summary: The triple La Nina of 2020-2022 severely impacted Eastern Australia. The prolonged period of above average and record rainfall caused multiple flood emergencies, saturated soils and triggered 1000’s of landslides across QLD and NSW, many with disastrous outcomes. This put immense pressure on under resourced government authorities to respond to landslide disasters. With necessary experience and resources hollowed out of the public sector, the challenges were mostly met by engaging the services of professional geotechnical consulting firms. Overall, the obstacles posed by these extreme weather events were arguably well managed with a large proportion of failures successfully remediated efficiently with cost effective solutions. Use of rapid slope risk assessments under the umbrella of the RMS Guide to Slope Risk Analysis and application of ALARP risk management principles providing controlled access to public infrastructure while events were unfolding became a feature of the coordinated response. However, in a few cases the system was found wanting with poorly justified extended road closures that have had devastating economic impacts on local communities and disproportionate, highly costly repairs that did not apply scarce public funds in the most cost-effective manner. This paper looks at two similar landslides in colluvial soils in the Sydney Basin that unfolded during 2022. While similar in their geological characteristics and risk attributes, these landslides had vastly different management outcomes: “Good” – Settlers Road, and “Bad and Ugly” – Wolgan Valley Road. These case studies provide lessons for management of landslide disasters in the future. papers.title: Soil Salinity under Climate Change in Pakistan: Emerging Challenges and Sustainable Management Approaches for Agriculture
papers.source: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
papers.summary: Soil salinity is a major constraint to agricultural productivity, soil health, and food security in Pakistan, particularly under changing climatic conditions. Rising temperatures, increased evapotranspiration, irregular precipitation, droughts, flooding, and sea-level rise can intensify salt accumulation and alter soil–water interactions. This review examines the emerging challenges associated with climate change and soil salinity in Pakistan, focusing on their impacts on soil properties, crop physiology, agricultural production, and rural livelihoods. It discusses the mechanisms of soil salinity and sodicity, their spatial distribution, and the interactions among climate variability, irrigation practices, groundwater quality, and secondary salinization. Furthermore, sustainable management approaches are evaluated, including gypsum application, organic amendments, integrated nutrient management, efficient irrigation, drainage improvement, and appropriate leaching strategies. Climate-resilient approaches, such as conventional crop breeding, modern biotechnology, halophyte utilization, plant growth-promoting microorganisms, and mycorrhizal associations, are also explored. The review highlights the potential of remote sensing, geographic information systems, precision agriculture, and predictive modelling to support salinity monitoring and site-specific management. Despite these opportunities, important challenges remain, including insufficient long-term monitoring, limited region-specific data, economic constraints, and gaps in farmer awareness and institutional coordination. Addressing these challenges requires integrated research, effective agricultural policies, improved extension services, and collaboration among researchers, policymakers, and farming communities. papers.title: Shallow landslide diagnostics for Southern California
papers.summary: Shallow landslides are significant natural hazards in the mountainous regions of Southern California during anomalously wet winter seasons, posing substantial risks to life and property. Better understanding and operational prediction of the atmospheric and land-surface conditions leading to the initiation of these impactful events are critical for mitigating life loss and reducing damage costs. This study aims to characterize and provide templates for operational prediction of the triggering conditions of shallow landslides in Southern California with the application of the MHEBC, a decade-long, high-resolution, prototype dataset of quantitative precipitation estimates. This dataset has region-specific calibration and is the result of methodologies tailored to capture the orographic signal of precipitation, which is a key element for the generation of the precipitation associated with landslide occurrence in this region. Using recorded landslide events from the California Geological Survey Reported Landslides Database, rainfall thresholds for landslide occurrence are derived on the basis of the MHEBC dataset. Significant quality control was necessary for both rainfall and landslide databases before high-quality data input could be provided for the analysis. Observed local landslide data availability is typically limited worldwide, and Southern California is no exception. For such conditions, estimates of landslide occurrence are obtained using manually-derived precipitation thresholds, following well defined operational procedures. In addition, a Random Forest (RF) machine-learning model and a few of its variants were applied to the same high quality but limited dataset to examine its utility for operational prediction under typically limited data. Under a variety of performance measures the automated RF does only marginally better than the well-established manual threshold procedure. papers.title: Shaking table investigation into seismic failure mechanisms of bedrock-underlain stratified slopes: influence of soil layer configuration
papers.summary: Soil layer configuration governs the seismic failure characteristics and dynamic responses of layered slopes. However, the seismic damage evolution and mechanical mechanisms of clay-over-sand and sand-over-clay slopes remain poorly understood. This study integrates shaking table tests and cyclic triaxial tests to investigate how soil layer distribution controls slope failure mode, acceleration amplification, and dynamic stress evolution. The results indicate that: (1) Differences in soil mechanical properties across layers give rise to distinct seismic damage patterns. The upper-clay/lower-sand slope exhibits progressive plastic sliding with significant accumulated deformation, whereas the upper-sand/lower-clay slope undergoes brittle failure characterized by surface tensile cracking and shallow instantaneous sliding. (2) The acceleration amplification factor increases nonlinearly with peak ground acceleration (PGA), peaking no later than the critical state and decreasing sharply once the slope fails, thereby serving as a precursor to seismically-induced slope instability. (3) Soil layer configuration governs the spatial evolution of dynamic stress. In the upper-clay/lower-sand slope, the soft clay layer in the upper-middle section exhibits large stress fluctuations and frequent redistribution, forming the primary damage zone. In the upper-sand/lower-clay slope, the lower clay layer serves as a stable basal boundary, intensifying dynamic stress responses in the middle-lower section; slope stability is governed by basal restraint. (4) Quantitative stress–volumetric strain constitutive models were developed from triaxial tests at varying confining pressures, elucidating the transition from dilative behavior at low pressures to contractive behavior at high pressures and revealing how confining pressure governs soil deformation and failure. papers.summary: ABSTRACT Accurate landslide susceptibility assessment in mountainous regions is often constrained by the reliance on static environmental factors and by spatial discontinuities in SBAS‐InSAR‐derived deformation caused by decorrelation. To address this widely encountered problem in vegetated and topographically complex landslide‐prone regions, this study proposes a potentially transferable workflow for static‐deformation‐informed landslide susceptibility assessment that integrates SBAS‐InSAR deformation reconstructed using a standard random forest (RF) regression model with ensemble machine learning. Wanzhou District, Chongqing, China, located within the Three Gorges Reservoir Area, was selected as a representative mountainous study area influenced by reservoir‐related hydrological processes. Mean line‐of‐sight deformation rates were retrieved from ascending Sentinel‐1A SAR images acquired between January 2020 and December 2024. Fifteen static conditioning factors and a historical landslide inventory were compiled, and RF regression was used to reconstruct deformation in low‐coherence areas. The reconstructed deformation field was then incorporated as a multi‐year deformation‐based conditioning factor into landslide susceptibility modelling. Four models, including RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, and Stacking, were developed under static‐only and static‐deformation‐informed scenarios. The results show that incorporating InSAR‐derived deformation generally improved model performance, with the InSAR–Stacking model achieving the highest AUC of 0.9082. Frequency ratio analysis indicated that historical landslides were more strongly concentrated in high‐ and very‐high‐susceptibility classes under the static‐deformation‐informed framework. papers.summary: Abstract Landslide susceptibility maps (LSMs) depict the spatial probability of landslide occurrence, typically using data-driven models based on past event distributions. However, these models often overlook temporal changes, assuming that past patterns reliably predict future events. In a rapidly changing world, influenced by factors such as climate change and urbanization, this assumption may lead to inconsistencies in LSMs over time, reducing their predictive accuracy. To investigate this issue, we analyzed a multi-temporal inventory of 1518 landslides over the past 70 years in Wanzhou District, China, a region impacted by significant environmental changes. We first examined the temporal and spatial variations in landslide patterns. Then, we employed random forest (RF) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithms to create five LSMs, each based on landslide data from different periods. Finally, we conducted a multi-temporal validation to evaluate the effectiveness of these maps in predicting landslides occurring in subsequent decades. Our findings reveal temporal shifts in landslide spatial patterns and changes in the model-derived importance of causal factors. These variations may be associated with changing environmental conditions in the study area. Both RF and XGBoost models produced LSMs with varying patterns depending on the temporal baseline of the landslide data used. Importantly, the accuracy of these maps decreases as the time span of the inventory data increases. Maps based on short-term data showed higher accuracy, but their predictive power declined rapidly over time, suggesting that in the context of significant environmental changes, LSMs need continuous updates and further spatiotemporal analysis to remain effective.

Deformation and reinforcement of piled bridge foundations on weathered mudstone slopes
papers.summary: Introduction: With the rapid development of China’s highway system, the construction of bridges spanning valleys in mountainous regions has become inevitable. In these areas, the deformation of bridge foundations must be strictly controlled, often through slopes reinforced with anti-slide piles. Materials and methods: Departing from the conventional “landslide–stabilizing pile” paradigm, this study adopts a holistic system perspective by modeling the “bridge pile–anti-sliding pile–weathered mudstone slope” as an integrated finite element method (FEM) framework, with the Qiezang Bridge on the Linxia–Dahejia Expressway as a case study. The horizontal displacement of the bridge foundation and anti-piles serves as the principal optimization target. Results: The installation of the rear-row anti-pile (P1) alone reduced the maximum horizontal displacement of the bridge foundation from 6.67 mm to 5.07 mm, corresponding to a 24.0% decrease. This confirms that a single-row configuration at the rear effectively enhances the deformation resistance of the foundation. By adjusting the location of the front-row anti-pile (P5) under the prevailing geological conditions, an optimal position of p x = 2.0 m was identified in the case of double anti-slide piles reinforcement. Conclusions: Comparative results indicate that the interaction between piles and soil is highly complex, due to the combined effects of lateral parabolic loads from soil thrust, lateral triangular loads from pile deflection, and soil resistance acting on the piles. Given the prevailing geological setting, the lateral displacement of P5 decreased from 51.2 mm to 34.0 mm at a position of p x = 2.0 m, representing a reduction of 17.2 mm (33.6%) and remaining the horizontal displacement of the bridge within the allowable limit. This provides a quantitative basis for reinforcing bridge foundations on weathered mudstone slopes.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Mapping Using a Random Forest Model on Google Earth Engine in Kuningan Regency
papers.summary: This study demonstrates that the Random Forest algorithm is effective in mapping landslide susceptibility in the Hantara area and its surrounding regions, as evidenced by strong model performance with an AUC value of 0.868, indicating a high capability to distinguish between landslide and non-landslide locations. Model evaluation shows an AUC value of 0.868, which reflects a strong discriminative performance in separating landslide locations from non-landslide areas. Analysis of variable importance highlights vegetation condition represented by OSAVI, soil physical characteristics indicated by clay content, and topographic parameters, particularly slope class and elevation, as the dominant factors influencing landslide susceptibility. In contrast, rainfall, geological conditions, and land use/land cover contribute as secondary controlling factors. The generated susceptibility probability values range from 0.193 to 0.787 and were subsequently classified into three susceptibility levels. The resulting map is predominantly characterized by the moderate susceptibility class, accounting for 50.46% of the study area, followed by the high (26.60%) and low (22.94%) susceptibility classes. These findings demonstrate that the integration of remote sensing–derived variables with the Random Forest approach provides a robust spatial analysis framework for supporting landslide risk mitigation and management in the study area.

papers.title: Scaling Water Bunds for Climate Resilience Management in Kenyan Rainfed Agri-Food Systems (SWaRM)
papers.source: CGSPace A Repository of Agricultural Research Outputs (Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research)
papers.summary: Kenya’s arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) face compounding pressures from land degradation, erratic rainfall, and recurrent drought. Water bunds, simple semi-circular earthen structures dug along contour lines to capture rainwater, reduce runoff, and regenerate vegetation, offer a proven nature-based response. The policy challenge is no longer whether water bunds work, but how to scale adoption efficiently and equitably across Kenya’s diverse tenure contexts and governance settings. The Scaling Water bunds for climate Resilience Management in Kenyan rainfed agri-food systems (SWaRM) project addresses this through a four-year bilateral research program funded by the Netherlands-CGIAR Water-Food Nexus Research Program (NWO). Led by IWMI in consortium with Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Tegemeo Institute, and Justdiggit, SWaRM combines economic analysis of adoption determinants, impact evaluation of co-designed scaling tools, and multi-stakeholder platform facilitation for evidence-to-policy translation. Findings are expected to inform Kenya’s Land Reclamation Policy and generate transferable lessons for scaling nature-based water retention solutions across sub-Saharan Africa’s drylands.

papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow numerical models are widely used for hazard assessment and engineering design, yet many models still treat bed evolution in a simplified or uncoupled manner. This study presents faDebrisFOAM, an open-source depth-averaged solver developed in OpenFOAM® that couples debris-flow motion, entrainment, deposition, and terrain evolution within a finite-area framework. The model represents the mixture as an equivalent fluid of variable density and incorporates mass exchanges with an erodible bed layer through entrainment and deposition laws. papers.title: Generalized Effective Stress Equation for Variably Saturated Frozen Soil
papers.source: Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract A unified effective stress equation for variably saturated frozen soil is proposed, theoretically verified, and experimentally evaluated. Cryostress, capillary suction stress, and adsorptive suction stress coexist when variably saturated soil is subject to freezing and thawing. Cryostress consists of three physically distinct forces at three interfaces: ice–ice bonding, ice–liquid capillary force, and ice–particle adsorptive force. Cryostress is a characteristic function of temperature and water content quantified by the cryostress characteristic curve. A generalized effective stress can be established by applying the principles of mechanical equilibrium and soil water potential equilibrium on the soil–water–ice–air representative element volume. A closed-form equation is developed where effective stress is equal to the total stress minus suction stress and cryostress. The generalized effective stress equation can be reduced to Bishop’s form of effective stress in saturated frozen soil when ice–particle adsorptive stress is neglected, to Lu and Likos’ suction stress-based effective stress in unfrozen unsaturated soil, and to Terzaghi’s effective stress in unfrozen saturated soil. The closed-form equation is experimentally evaluated using published shear strength test results for sandy soil, lean clay, and silty clay. The fitted parameters also show good consistency with independently measured soil water and soil freezing characteristic curves for lean clay. The proposed framework offers a practical and unified approach to describe the strength of variably saturated frozen soils.

The results show that the LFFDF cascade operates as asymmetric transition processes, in which the dominant controls are state‐dependent. Rainfall‐induced landslides supplied one‐third of the mobilized sediment; their interaction with flash floods increased channel‐flow Shields stress by more than an order of magnitude, prematurely initiating debris flows in headwater channels. The downstream reversion from debris flow to flash flood is mainly controlled by the thickness and saturation state of channel sediments. Finally, we suggest a cascade‐based paradigm for risk assessment to enhance community resilience to LFFDF risks.

However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

This study proposes an optimization method for calibrating landslide rheological parameters based on random forest (RF) and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Firstly, a dynamic numerical model of landslide is established using three-dimensional model DAN (DAN3D). Then, the lateral accumulation width and the longitudinal runout distance at different spatial locations across the deposit are integrated to calibrate the rheological parameters. Next, the NSGA-II algorithm is employed to obtain the Pareto solutions of rheological parameters by minimizing the prediction errors of lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at each location. To avoid extensive repetitive DAN3D simulations within NSGA-II, RF-based surrogate models are established to estimate the lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at different spatial locations. The final optimal rheological parameters are objectively selected from Pareto solutions by the entropy weight method (EWM). Finally, the proposed approaches are illustrated and validated using two landslides that occurred in Gansu Province, China. Results indicated that rheological parameters optimized by the proposed approaches not only can accurately characterize the endangered area of historical events, but also provide reasonable forward prediction of runout behavior of similar landslide events with desired accuracy. RF surrogate models can remove the computational burden within NSGA-II. Integrating both the lateral accumulation width and longitudinal runout distance into the calibration of rheological parameters can improve the prediction accuracy of landslide endangered area.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslide hazards along the Banihal–Ramban corridor of the Jammu–Srinagar National Highway (NH-44) represent a critical geoenvironmental challenge in Northwestern Himalaya, where active tectonics, fragile lithology, steep terrain, and increasing extreme precipitation interact with intensive infrastructure development. This technical note presents a focused analysis of flash floods and landslides of April 20, 2025, examining their triggering mechanisms, cascading geomorphic processes, and impacts on transportation infrastructure and settlements. Historical landslide records (1990–2025) and regional hydroclimatic observations are incorporated to contextualize the event within evolving patterns of hazard frequency and anthropogenic slope modification along the NH-44 corridor. The April 2025 disaster resulted from the localized high-intensity precipitation, which elevated pore-water pressures, reduced slope stability, and triggered multiple failures in structurally weakened rock formations. Results highlight a transition from isolated slope failures toward compound and cascading hazard scenarios involving flash floods, debris flows, and infrastructure disruption. The study underscores the increasing vulnerability of this strategic Himalayan lifeline. It emphasizes the need for geologically informed engineering design, improved drainage management, and integrated early warning strategies to enhance long-term resilience.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. However, practical landslide detection faces challenges including limited data, high computation, large memory use, and low accuracy. In this study, high-quality landslide remote sensing images were collected from southeastern Xizang to construct a landslide remote sensing data set. To address the issue of insufficient samples, an improved model, landslide-deep convolutional generative adversarial network (L-DCGAN), based on DCGAN, was proposed to enhance landslide remote sensing data. The enhanced data set was constructed by incorporating efficient channel attention (ECA) and squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules into the generator and discriminator, respectively. Additionally, an improved YOLOv8 model, landslide-you only look once version 8(L-YOLOv8), was proposed. First, the cross-stage partial pyramid convolution (CSPPC) and grouped and shuffled convolution (GSConv) modules replaced the cross stage partial layer with 2 branches (C2f) module and ordinary convolution in the network to reduce the number of model parameters and computational complexity. Then, the spatial and channel synergistic attention (SCSA) mechanism was introduced to improve detection accuracy. Experimental results showed that compared with the original YOLOv8 algorithm, the number of model parameters in L-YOLOv8 was reduced by approximately 41.78%, and the average accuracy on the landslide sample data set was increased by 0.57%, and frames per second (FPS) was improved by 33.87%. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

The combined use of statistical modeling, hydrologic factors, and geotechnical verification improves the reliability of landslide susceptibility assessment and provides a practical framework that can be applied in other mountainous regions affected by rainfall-induced landslides.

papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.summary: This doctoral research explored the application of Geographic Information System (GIS) and Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) techniques to improve soil mapping processes and support land management and biodiversity conservation, in alignment with the objectives of the National Biodiversity Future Center (NBFC). The study was conducted in two Regional Parks of the Northern Apennines, a region characterized by high environmental heterogeneity and a rich cartographic heritage. Traditional pedological knowledge and expert-driven selection of environmental covariates were first employed to delineate land units and produce a conventional soil map. Subsequently, DSM approaches using Random Forest models with recursive feature elimination were applied to generate an alternative soil map based on DEM derivatives and remotely sensed data, achieving high accuracy and interpretability. The analysis identified key drivers of soil differentiation, such as topography, insolation, vegetation indices, and proximity to water bodies, highlighting their potential for transferability to similar areas and for overcoming cartographic discontinuities. Complementary studies on the same area revealed that climate exerts a stronger influence than vegetation on soil evolution, and that considering soil diversity enhances understanding of organic matter dynamics. The second component of this research addressed the reestablishment of chestnut cultivation in the Northern Apennines through a land suitability model that was tested on the municipality of Castel del Rio (BO).
