papers.title: Analisis Kerawanan Longsorlahan di Kabupaten Wonogiri Berdasarkan Sistem Informasi Geografis
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
authors: , Dr. Annisa Trisnia Sasmi, S.Si., M.T
papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Each parameter was assigned a score and weight, followed by an overlay process to generate a landslide susceptibility map. Validation was conducted using 85 landslide occurrence points from 2025, obtained from the Wonogiri Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), with 12 of these points verified through field surveys. The results indicate that landslide susceptibility is categorized into four classes: low, moderate, high, and very high. The moderate susceptibility class covers the largest area. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

papers.summary: With advances in satellite technology, spaceborne data are becoming available to the public and scientific community at increasing temporal and spatial resolutions. The study area is set in the northwest Argentinean Andes -- a region particularly susceptible to mass movement processes due to steep topography, heavy rainfall during the summer monsoon, and geologic pre-conditioning. GNSS field measurements were employed to validate the derived elevations and identify optimal processing parameters. papers.title: Assessing the influence of rainfall-induced desiccation cracking on slope stability in Malaysia
papers.summary: The influence of climate change on slope stability has become increasingly relevant in recent years, particularly in tropical regions like Malaysia, where the frequency and severity of rainfall events are anticipated to vary considerably. This study examined the combined impacts of rainfall variability and soil desiccation cracking on the slope stability in Malaysia’s tropical granitic residual soils. The study conducted a comprehensive analysis of precipitation patterns utilizing both historical and projected climatic data across multiple climate change scenarios. It subsequently investigated the formation of desiccation cracks in soils exposed to repeated cycles of wetting and drying under controlled laboratory circumstances, replicating actual seasonal variations. Numerical models evaluated the impact of rainfall infiltration on slope stability amid changing climatic circumstances. The rainfall pattern analysis revealed a notable tendency of increasing wet-season rainfall but a considerable decline in dry-season precipitation. This extreme climate condition has provoked the formation of desiccation cracks on soil slopes. The subsequent experimental study indicated that desiccation cracks substantially enhance water infiltration into the soil. The mechanism involved increased crack formation with the repetitive wetting-drying cycles, leading to increased void ratio in soil, and hence resulted in a higher permeability. papers.summary: (English) Hydro-geomorphological hazards such as floods and rainfall-induced landslides frequently co-occur in mountainous regions, driven by shared meteorological forcing but governed by distinct hydrological and geotechnical mechanisms. papers.title: Engineering geological properties of the Awhitu Group sands at Muriwai, New Zealand
papers.summary: Landslides are a critical risk to New Zealand’s infrastructure and economy, as evidenced during the widespread early 2023 storms. Muriwai, a settlement in the Auckland region, has an 80 m escarpment consisting of Awhitu Group sands that failed as fatal landslides during strong rainfall in early 2023 and in 1965. Interestingly, there is currently limited research on the geotechnical properties of the Awhitu Group sands, particularly at Muriwai. papers.summary: Background: Landslides are a natural disaster that often occurs in Indonesia, particularly in areas with steep slopes and high rainfall. papers.summary: This study developed a landslide susceptibility modelling framework for the Nihotupu reservoir system, located in the Waitākere Ranges, Auckland, New Zealand, to evaluate how different spatial representations of terrain influence model performance and susceptibility mapping. Three mapping unit scenarios were implemented: pixel-based, slope-unit-based, and 20 m buffer-based representations of the terrain. papers.title: A framework for spatio-temporal assessment of slope stability along mountainous transport corridors
papers.summary: Globally, research on the interaction between roads and landslides has largely focused on roads as triggering factors. Existing susceptibility assessments typically represent roads through static conditioning factors such as distance to road or road density, while limited attention has been given to how road infrastructure itself responds to dynamic slope processes. Consequently, their outputs often lack practical relevance for infrastructure resilience, particularly under evolving climate and environmental conditions. The aim of this research is to develop a dynamic, spatio-temporal framework that integrates hydrological conditions with slope stability analysis to assess landslide susceptibility along transport corridors. The framework was applied to the 24.7 km long Mukamira'Kabaya road and its 16.8 km² surrounding corridor in northwestern Rwanda, a steep environment frequently affected by shallow rainfall-induced landslides. papers.title: Analisis Tingkat Kerawanan Longsor Lahan Di Kecamatan Ile Ape Timur Kabupaten Lembata Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Timur (NTT)
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslides are a common natural disaster in areas with steep topography, including Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict, Lembata Regency, East Nusa Tenggara. This disaster is caused by a combination of natural factors, such as high rainfall, slope gradients, soil types, and human activities that alter land use. This study aims to analyze the landslide susceptibility levels and identify mitigation efforts in Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict. This research employed a descriptive method with a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. The data used included slope gradient maps, soil type maps, rainfall data, and land use maps, analyzed using a weighted overlay technique to produce a landslide susceptibility map. Primary data were collected through field observations, while secondary data were obtained from relevant agencies such as BPBD and PUPR of Lembata Regency. The results show that the landslide susceptibility levels in Ile Ape Timur are categorized into four classes: not susceptible (3,174 hectares), less susceptible (25 hectares), susceptible (718 hectares), and highly susceptible (6 hectares). The main factors influencing susceptibility are steep slopes, Andosols soil prone to erosion, and relatively high annual rainfall. Recommended mitigation efforts include structural approaches, such as terracing and the installation of early warning systems (EWS), as well as non-structural approaches, including community education and disaster simulations. This study is expected to serve as a basis for the government and local communities to implement effective landslide disaster mitigation measures, minimizing material losses and casualties.

papers.title: Understanding the rainfall triggering post-fire debris flows in California
papers.summary: Post-fire debris flows (PFDFs) are a cascading hazard resulting from the interaction between intense rainfall and susceptible terrain altered by wildfire. These events have proven devastating in the past, damaging infrastructure and communities, particularly in California, where fire season in the warm months is closely followed by rainfall during the cool season. The expansion of wildfire occurrence, along with pronounced variability in terrain and climate across California, highlights the need to better understand the rainfall conditions associated with this hazard under both current and future climates. Consequently, this dissertation integrates multiple datasets and methods to characterize rainfall and atmospheric conditions associated with storms triggering post-fire debris flows, providing new insight into the rainfall environments, precipitation-system structure, predictive controls, and future changes in PFDF hazard across California. First, an inventory of PFDF is compiled and used to characterize rainfall conditions associated with event occurrence using nearby rain gauges, including storm duration, rainfall accumulation, antecedent rainfall, and short-duration peak intensity. papers.title: Development of an advanced computational approach for early warning and predictions of rainfall-induced slope failures
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most common natural hazards, threatening lives, homes, and infrastructure worldwide. This research develops a novel approach to predict landslides and provide early warning, even when field data are limited. The study creates advanced computer models that represent real soil conditions and simulate how slopes respond to heavy rainfall. These physics-based models are then combined with machine learning that learn continuously from monitoring data, allowing predictions to be updated and refined over time. By improving prediction accuracy, this research supports more effective landslide early warning systems and helps reduce damage and loss of life.

papers.title: Analisis Spasial Kerawanan Longsor untuk Penentuan Titik Shelter di Kecamatan Petungkriyono Kabupaten Pekalongan
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility is a condition that indicates the level of potential for an area to experience landslides which is influenced by factors such as slope gradient, rainfall, soil type, geology, and land use. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility for determining shelter points in Petungkriyono District, Pekalongan Regency using a GIS (Geographic Information System)-based overlay method with ArcGIS 10.8 software. The data used include landslide occurrence data, DEMNAS Indonesia, RBI Indonesia, rainfall in 2014–2025, land use in 2025, distribution of disaster mitigation shelters, soil type, and geology of Petungkriyono District. The results of the study indicate that the level of landslide susceptibility in Petungkriyono District is dominated by high class with an area of 6930.5 Ha or 84.58%, medium class with an area of 1228.3 Ha or 14.99%, and low class with an area of 34.9 Ha or 0.43%. In general, every village in Petungkriyono District is characterized by high landslide vulnerability. Curugmuncar Village is the most vulnerable area, with a high vulnerability percentage reaching 96.68%. Disaster mitigation shelters are divided into four types: government, education, health, and worship shelters. There are three government shelters, 14 education shelters, one health shelter, and 27 worship shelters spread across all villages in Petungkriyono District.

papers.title: RAINFALL-INDUCED LANDSLIDE SUSCEPTIBILITY MODELLING FOR PREDICTION AND EARLY WARNING
papers.source: CINECA IRIS Institutional Research information system (University of Urbino)
papers.summary: Landslide detection and prediction rely on Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) as well as historical documentation of past events. Utilizing multiple elevation datasets and a landslide inventory, logical optimization methods to partition terrain into Slope Units (SUs) used as modelling units for landslide prediction is introduced. Landslide area, counts as well as terrain characteristics like homogeneous slope aspect are used and later unified into segmentation metrics to assess their performance in landslide susceptibility models. These terrain units are continued to be used in dynamic landslide susceptibility modelling through Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to approach real-time landslide warnings for disaster and risk management. Particularly for rainfall-induced landslides, the integration of rainfall as a dynamic covariate in statistical modelling is approached. Keeping the selection of the mapping unit to SUs, first we utilize cumulative antecedent rainfall information by testing multiple time-windows to select the most-representative temporal bracket for the region. Secondly, while the first technique still remains using rainfall in a scalar form, we implement a functional GAM to utilize the time-series information and present rainfall as a temporally dynamic variable. The model performances undergo a number of validation techniques and the drawbacks of lacking information is explained with varying prediction power. These enhances in methodologies are presented to support Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) for disaster risk and mitigation measures.

Predictive slope stability models play a key role in improving community resilience to this widespread hazard. However, several limitations still constrain the prediction of rainfall-induced landslides at a regional scale. While numerous predictive models have been developed, most struggle to balance mechanistic rigor, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency for regional-scale assessments. Many rely on simplified mechanistic assumptions, while others use empirical approaches that lack any physical basis. Even when more rigorous mechanistic models exist, high computational costs, limited scalability, and sensitivity to input availability and quality affect their performance. CRISIS integrates a pseudo-three-dimensional slope stability approach with a hydrological model selected by the user, here implemented with the Parallel Integrated Hydrologic Model (ParFlow). papers.title: The influence of the Critical Zone on hillslope hydrology and stability
papers.source: Institutional Research Information System (Università degli Studi di Trento)
papers.summary: The Earth's near-surface layer, which extends from the vegetation canopy to unweathered bedrock, is known as the Critical Zone (CZ). It is essential for regulating the incidence of hydrological processes and hydro-geo hazards. Enhancing predictive models of infiltration, discharge production, and landslide initiation, requires an understanding of the relationships between the CZ and hillslope hydrology. In this research, the impact of changes in CZ configuration and characteristics on hillslope hydrology and stability is examined in various geomorphological and climatic contexts. The research begins by investigating rainfall infiltration mechanisms in the stratified pyroclastic soil-mantled slopes of the Campania region, Southern Italy. Field monitoring, laboratory infiltration experiments, and physically based hydrological modeling were combined to reproduce observed pore-water pressures, soil-moisture dynamics, and subsurface flow mechanisms. The findings enhanced our understanding of rainfall-induced slope instability and provided further insights into the redistribution of water in layered volcanic deposits. The work expands by using a coupled hydro-mechanical framework to forecast the onset of shallow landslides. The framework combines i) a transient hydrological model with ii) a finite element solver for slope stability in order to iii) compute local field factors of safety (LFS) under dynamic rainfall conditions. papers.summary: This study analyses the hazard related to shallow landslides in north-western Tuscany, specifically focusing on the Middle Serchio Valley and the northern area of the city of Lucca. The primary objective is to define critical rainfall thresholds to enhance local early warning systems. Using R software, statistical techniques including logistic regression, least squares, and quantile regression were applied to two datasets: a historical one (1937–2010; Giannecchini et al., 2012) and a recent one (2010–2025). The analysis reveals that the new local thresholds are less conservative than regional and national ones, effectively reducing false alarms by better reflecting the specific morphological and hydrological characteristics of the study area. A comparative analysis of the historical dataset shows threshold curve slopes consistent with previous studies, although current statistical models exhibit slightly higher intercepts. In the recent dataset, a less distinct graphical separation between landslide-triggering and non-triggering rainfall events was observed; this phenomenon is likely attributable to the limited sample size, which, while minimizing false alarms, increases vulnerability to missed alarms. A significant finding is the integration of antecedent rainfall, a parameter that substantially refined the model's predictive efficiency. This work provides a fundamental methodological and practical contribution to the prediction of rainfall-induced hydrogeological risk.

papers.summary: Boreal peatlands store carbon and regulate hydrology because saturation slows decomposition and allows peat to accumulate. Roads interrupt these controls by compressing peat and blocking lateral groundwater flow, producing persistent changes in water-table position, oxygen exposure, solute movement, and decomposition. As road removal and peatland reclamation become more common, restoration must be guided by how disturbance continues to affect ecosystem function below ground, rather than only whether vegetation or surface hydrology appear to recover. The first aspect of this thesis examined how a mineral access road altered hydrophysical structure, peat compression, and chemistry across depth in a moderate-rich treed fen near Slave Lake, Alberta. Road loading compressed and displaced peat horizons, while reduced hydraulic conductivity beneath the road divided the site into wetter upgradient and drier downgradient zones. These hydrological contrasts were consistent with differences in nutrient transport, ionic conditions, and decomposition patterns. Because subsurface compression can persist after mineral fill is removed, restoration planning must address both lateral hydrological reconnection and the altered vertical arrangement of peat that controls water storage, redox conditions, and substrate availability. The second aspect of this thesis followed up on these findings by asking whether the same changes in peat structure and organic matter chemistry also affect molecular monitoring. DNA-based methods can identify microbial responses before visible ecosystem recovery, but only when extraction differences reflect biological conditions rather than peat chemistry. papers.title: Effects of root architecture of different wheat cultivars on soil structure
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Plant roots play a crucial role in maintaining soil health by influencing physical structure and hydraulic properties. This study investigates relationships between root morphology of wheat genotypes and their impacts on soil structure and hydraulic characteristics. Using shovelomics, we characterized root systems of wheat cultivars (Paragon, Bologna) and landraces (Senatore-Cappelli, Watkins238) selected for contrasting root morphologies. X-ray computed tomography (CT) was applied to examine soil pore networks at cylinder and aggregate scales, while soil hydraulic properties were measured using Wind evaporation and dew point techniques. Results demonstrated significant genotype-driven differences in soil morphology and hydraulic functions. Structural analyses (Minkowski functionals, percolation theory) showed significant variability in bioporosity and pore connectivity among genotypes compared to bare soil. Senatore-Cappelli exhibited notably larger biopores (>1 mm diameter). Hydraulic characterization using a van Genuchten bimodal model revealed statistically significant differences in soil water retention curves and hydraulic conductivity among genotypes. Root traits, including total root length, branching frequency, lateral root length, and root diameter, significantly correlated with soil pore size distribution and hydraulic parameters. This analysis underscores the importance of root architecture in modulating soil structure and water dynamics, highlighting the potential of specific wheat genotypes to affect soil health, water retention, and agricultural sustainability.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF DOLOMITE AMENDMENTS ON PER- AND POLYFLUOROALKYL SUBSTANCES (PFAS) LEACHING IN AGRICULTURAL SOILS
papers.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are often found in agricultural soils due to land application of biosolids, wastewater-derived materials, and atmospheric deposition. However, PFAS transport behavior in variably saturated agricultural soils remains poorly studied. This study evaluates PFAS mobility within unsaturated soil using both intact soil cores (diameter: 3 inches, referred to as large columns (LC)) and packed, homogeneous soil columns (diameter: 1 inch, referred to as small columns (SC)) under the presence and absence of dolomite, which was recently reported to be able to reduce PFAS mobility through adsorption. All columns were amended with a biosolid (Milorganite) and half of the large and small columns received a powdered dolomite amendment at the surface. Columns were subjected to episodic infiltration based on precipitation data from 2019, and the leachate was collected at the base of each column for PFAS analysis. Our results showed that (1) the leaching of PFAS was strongly dependent on the structure and properties of the PFAS, and (2) dolomite amendments could lower the leaching of PFAS. The findings from this research will improve our quantitative understanding of how PFAS move through agricultural soils and the potential risks associated with land application, as well as the design and implementation of science-based management practices and regulation frameworks.

papers.title: Effect of dispersed clay and soil pore size on the hydraulic conductivity of soils irrigated with saline-sodic water
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: A shortage of good quality water has led to the use of low quality, high saline-sodic water that was considered unsuitable for irrigation purposes in the past. This can limit crop growth in the long term through the impacts on water and nutrient availability. Most studies use reductions in soil Ks as an indicator of soil pore blockage when saline-sodic irrigation water is used. However, the use of saline-sodic irrigation water requires improved understanding of the of cation exchange processes, soil structural degradation and the potential for soil pore blockage. In order to address this three laboratory trials were conducted to investigate the effect of soil pore size on soil cation exchange processes, dispersed clay movement and the mechanisms of soil pore blockage in relation to changes in soil Ks. An initial study was conducted on two soils packed into soil cores at two different bulk densities (ρb) and leached with solutions containing varying concentrations of clay sediments. This confirmed that soil pore size has a significant effect on dispersed clay movement and potential soil pore blockage. papers.title: Understanding preferential water flow and its contribution to inrush hazard susceptibility in block cave mining : an integrated modelling approach
papers.summary: Water infiltration dynamics in block cave mining are critical to understanding and managing inrush hazards that threaten mine safety and operational continuity. Primary water sources, groundwater aquifers, water-bearing faults, and surface water entering through the subsidence crater interact within the cave muck pile through preferential flow pathways that develop and evolve during mining. How that water then partitions within the broken ore column has received less attention. This research investigates the development and flow behaviour of these pathways using an integrated physical and numerical modelling approach. A conceptual model of a draw column is proposed and tested, characterized by central compressive plug flow zones (PFZ) bounded by finer-grained shear bands (SB1, SB2) that respond differently under unsaturated and saturated conditions. A 76-day quasi-two-dimensional physical experiment, instrumented with seven dielectric moisture sensors and a continuous load-cell mass balance, was complemented by a continuum-flow simulation in MIN3P-HPC, providing an independent benchmark of the within-medium hydraulic behaviour. The fines-rich shear bands retain three to three-and-a-half times the moisture content of the surrounding plug flow zones across all applied flux conditions. Sensor integration and continuum simulation give consistent end-of-experiment within-medium storage of 10.5-11.7 L and 11.75 L, respectively. papers.title: Study on hydraulic conductivity behaviour with regard to soil characteristics in landfill performance
papers.summary: Municipal solid waste generation continues to increase in Malaysia, placing greater demands on landfill containment systems to effectively prevent leachate migration and protect groundwater resources. The engineering performance of compacted landfill liners depends largely on the hydraulic conductivity achieved after compaction, which is governed by the combined influence of soil physical properties and compaction behaviour. However, the hydraulic performance of landfill-sourced residual soils in Malaysia remains insufficiently understood, particularly regarding the interaction between soil characteristics and hydraulic conductivity under realistic moisture and loading conditions. papers.title: Integrating ecohydrological, isotopic, and numerical approaches to assess water use by montane Scots pine under varying wetness conditions
papers.summary: (English) Ecohydrology provides a critical framework for understanding interactions between vegetation and the hydrological cycle, particularly in forested ecosystems that strongly regulate water fluxes and ecosystem resilience. In Mediterranean mountain regions, increasing climate variability and recurrent droughts place forests close to their hydraulic limits. Despite these mounting pressures, key uncertainties remain regarding how trees access, store, and utilize water across contrasting wetness conditions, and how these processes can be represented in ecohydrological models. This thesis investigates tree water uptake dynamics and their representation by integrating high temporal- and spatial-resolution field observations, stable water isotopes, and process-based modeling. The study was conducted in the Vallcebre Research Catchments (NE Spain), focusing on Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.). Field observations combined meteorological measurements, sap flow and stem diameter variations, soil water content and potential, groundwater levels, and weekly water stable isotopes sampling of precipitation, soil water, groundwater, and xylem water. These data were analyzed using statistical approaches and numerical modeling to examine tree water uptake at the plot scale during contrasting dry and wet periods. papers.summary: Understanding subsurface water movement, particularly preferential water flow, is critical for water resource management and predicting contaminant transport. However, traditional invasive methods like dye staining experiments are destructive and only provide static information. papers.summary: In the context of the current climate crisis, the intensification of extreme meteoro-logical events necessitates a shift in hydrogeological risk-mitigation strategies, promoting a transition toward Nature-Based Solutions (NBS). Among these, Soil and Water Bioengineer-ing (SWBE) represent a bioinspired solution for slope stabilisation, as it combines geotech-nical safety with the restoration of ecological functionality. papers.title: Numerical simulation of the LRI process - Impregnation with a liquid resin of a real digitized reinforcement - Unsaturated flows and virtual permeability
papers.summary: Composite materials have become indispensable in numerous high performance applications, ranging from aerospace and automotive to sporting goods, due to their customized properties, such as high strength-to-weight ratios and design flexibility. The increasing demand for lightweight and high-strength materials to meet performance and sustainability targets has driven significant advancements in composite manufacturing technologies. papers.summary: There is increasing pressure in the UK to adopt alternative, sustainable uses for agricultural land. papers.summary: Slope failures cause severe human and economic losses worldwide, yet conventional stability methods describe them only up to the onset of failure. papers.title: Managing the effect of infiltration variability on the performance of surface irrigation
papers.source: University of Southern Queensland ePrints (University of Southern Queensland)
papers.summary: Infiltration variability is a major issue during the design phase and management for all types of irrigation systems. papers.summary: The performance of surface irrigation is a function of the field design, infiltration characteristic of the soil, and the irrigation management practice. However, the complexity of the interactions makes it difficult for irrigators to identify optimal design or management practices. The infiltration characteristic of the soil is the most crucial of all the factors affecting the performance of surface irrigation and both spatial and temporal variations in the infiltration characteristic are a major physical constraint to achieving higher irrigation application efficiencies. Real-time optimisation and control has the potential to overcome these spatial and temporal variations and return highly significant improvements in performance. Calculation of the infiltration parameters from irrigation advance data is now the preferred method. If the process is to be included in a real time control system it must be done accurately, reliably and rapidly, and with a minimum of field data. Substantial work has been directed towards developing methods to estimate the infiltration characteristics of soil from irrigation advance data. However, none of the existing methods are entirely suitable for use in real time control. The greatest limitation is that they are data intensive and or unreliable and provide soil infiltration properties after an irrigation event. A simple real-time control system for furrow irrigation is proposed that: predicts the infiltration characteristics of the soil in real-time using data measured during an irrigation event, simulates the irrigation, and determines the optimum time to cut-off for that irrigation. The basis of the system is a new method for the Real-time Estimation of the Infiltration Parameters (REIP) under furrow irrigation, developed during this research study, and that uses a model infiltration curve, and a scaling process to predict the infiltration characteristics for each furrow and each irrigation event. papers.title: Boundary Influence in Truncated Groundwater Models: Reconstructing a Local-Scale MODFLOW Model from a Consultant-Developed Regional Model in the Monterey Subbasin
papers.summary: Regional groundwater models built by consultants contain valuable calibrated frameworks but are often too large and complex for repeated local-scale analysis. Rather than rebuilding an entirely new smaller model, this study truncates the existing consultant-built regional model of the Monterey Subbasin, preserving the original grid structure and parameter framework while reducing the active domain to a manageable size for planning-level use. A key finding is that boundary-condition representation exerted a dominant influence on simulated groundwater behavior within the truncated domain, highlighting that truncation is a structural decision that meaningfully affects how the model responds. Model performance was evaluated two ways. Alternative hydraulic conductivity fields derived from AEM resistivity data were used to assess how sensitive the reconstructed model was to changes in internal parameter structure. Transient injection simulations produced cumulative groundwater mounding that grew progressively over repeated seasonal cycles, confirming realistic aquifer behavior and demonstrating the model's value as a practical and transparent planning-level tool.

papers.title: CAPILLARY-DRIVEN TRANSPORT IN POROUS MEDIA: UNSATURATED FLOW, THERMAL EFFECTS, AND VADOSE-ZONE CYCLING
papers.summary: Capillary-driven transport in porous media plays a fundamental role in a wide range of natural and engineered systems, including heat pipes, fibrous and ceramic materials, soils, contaminant transport in the vadose zone, and moisture-management technologies. Although substantial progress has been made in modeling and characterizing wicking under simplified conditions, important gaps remain in understanding how thermal gradients, partial saturation, and evaporation-driven solute cycling influence liquid transport in porous media. This dissertation addresses these gaps through a combined experimental, analytical, and numerical investigation of capillary-driven flow in porous materials across thermal, engineered, and environmental settings.The first part of this dissertation develops a Richards equation-based numerical framework to model moisture infusion in porous ceramics and other engineered materials by incorporating capillary pressure–saturation and relative permeability relationships. The model was validated against high-resolution neutron microscope imaging experiments and two independent analytical solutions. Extended simulations were then performed to investigate the role of engineered wettability — including hydrophilic surface coatings and hydrophobic inclusions — on two-dimensional moisture migration patterns. These results demonstrate how material design and local wettability modification can be used to control liquid transport pathways in porous systems. The second part of this work investigates non-isothermal wicking in porous media. Experiments were conducted using sintered polymer-bead wicks and hydrocarbon liquids under imposed temperature differences between the liquid and the wick. A sharp-front Darcy-based framework was developed to model the transient rise of liquid while accounting for temperature-dependent viscosity, surface tension, and density. papers.title: Impacts of Cover Crops, No-Tillage and Cotton-Sorghum Rotation on Soil-Water Dynamics: Environmental and Economic Implications
papers.summary: Water scarcity associated with declining groundwater levels in the Ogallala Aquifer threatens the long-term sustainability of irrigated agriculture in the semi-arid Texas High Plains. As irrigation capacity decreases, management strategies that improve soil-mediated water capture and enhance production resilience are increasingly important. This thesis integrates a regional literature synthesis with field-based evaluation of conservation practices aimed at improving water-use efficiency in cotton-based cropping systems. The literature identifies irrigation technology improvements, precision agriculture technologies, and soil health management as key pathways for reducing water demand and enhancing precipitation capture, while also emphasizing economic constraints and site-specific performance of conservation practices. A two-year field study assessed the short-term effects of cover crops and cotton–sorghum rotation under no-tillage on soil physical properties, crop productivity, and economic indicators. Soil measurements included saturated hydraulic conductivity, aggregate stability, compaction, and total organic carbon, alongside cotton and sorghum yield and fiber quality. Results showed limited short-term changes in most soil properties, although aggregate stability increased under rotational systems with cover crops. Cotton yield remained consistent across treatments, but fiber quality and associated economic returns declined in rotation-based systems. Sorghum performance was largely influenced by interannual climatic variability rather than management effects. Overall, findings suggest that while conservation practices hold potential to improve soil function and water-use efficiency, measurable agronomic and economic benefits may require long-term adoption. Extended evaluation is necessary to determine whether gradual soil health improvements can enhance system resilience and profitability under increasing water limitations.

papers.summary: Arsenic contamination in groundwater represents a critical environmental and public health challenge due to its high toxicity and widespread occurrence in natural aquifers. Chronic exposure to arsenic, even at trace levels, is associated with severe health effects, including skin lesions and increased cancer risk. Conventional treatment technologies, such as adsorption using activated carbon or metal oxides, often suffer from limited selectivity, regeneration difficulty, and reduced efficiency under varying pH conditions. Therefore, developing advanced sorbent materials with high capacity, selectivity, and structural stability is essential for addressing arsenic pollution in decentralized water systems.Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have recently emerged as promising materials for water purification owing to their tunable pore structures, high surface areas, and functional versatility. Among them, zirconium-based MOFs such as UiO-66 are particularly attractive because of their excellent water stability and Zr–OH active sites favorable for arsenate binding. However, the powdered nature of most MOFs presents significant challenges for practical filtration applications, including clogging, high pressure drop, and regeneration difficulties. To overcome these limitations, this work first focused on integrating UiO-66 and UiO-66-NH₂ with granular activated carbon (GAC) to develop hybrid point-of-use filtration materials. The composite exhibited uniform MOF attachment on GAC surfaces, mitigating issues related to powder handling and mobility. Batch adsorption tests revealed that UiO-66–GAC outperformed UiO-66-NH₂–GAC under near-neutral pH, highlighting the influence of surface chemistry on arsenic affinity. papers.summary: Hydraulic anisotropy in unsaturated soils significantly influences rainfall-induced slope failures, yet limited research has characterized its variation with depth. This study examines the hydraulic anisotropy of a layered unsaturated soil profile from 0.5m to 3.0m depth at 0.5m intervals and quantifies its impact on slope stability under transient infiltration. Laboratory characterization included index properties, Soil-Water Characteristic Curve (SWCC) and saturated permeability measurements for both vertical and horizontal flow directions. Results revealed consistent hydraulic anisotropy (Kr = Kₕ/Kv) ranging from 1.15 to 1.91 across depths, with highest anisotropy near the surface decreasing with depth due to overburden compression. Fines content exhibited a strong inverse relationship with permeability, reaching a minimum of 1.61×10−8 m/s at 1.5m depth where fines peaked at 59%. Numerical modeling using GeoStudio (SEEP/W and SLOPE/W) simulated 12-day rainfall (20 mm/day) followed by 12-day evaporation for 30° and 45° slopes under isotropic and anisotropic conditions. Results demonstrate that anisotropic conditions consistently produced lower factors of safety than isotropic assumptions at the critical Day 12 minimum, with the most pronounced effect observed on the 30° slope with a shallow slip surface, where anisotropy reduced the FoS by approximately 27.3%. For 45° slopes, reductions of 6.6% and 7.3% were recorded for deep-seated and shallow surfaces respectively, while the 30° deep- seated case showed a negligible difference of less than 1.0%. This research highlights that incorporating depth-dependent anisotropic hydraulic properties is essential for accurate rainfall- induced slope failure assessment.

Currently, the retaining system of the conventional configuration is mainly controlled by the geogrid. However, the embedment length of the geogrid requires massive excavation which also leads to the longer construction duration. Considering this limitation, reducing the length of the geogrid while maintaining sufficient stability became the primary objective of this study. On the other hand, although earth nailing systems have been widely applied in slope stabilization practice, integration between geogrid reinforcement and earth mechanical anchorage has not been demonstrated within a unified framework. ABAQUS was used to perform mechanical analysis calibrated from PLAXIS 2D for modified models with J-pin attachments. papers.title: Finite Element Method Simulations of Redox Processes in Nanoporous Gold and in Lithium Batteries
papers.source: Carl von Ossiezky University of Oldenburg
papers.summary: This thesis investigates the transport phenomena in nanoporous electrodes and in lithium electrodes using a combination of scanning electrochemical microscopy (SECM) and finite element method (FEM) simulations. The primary goal is to develop and validate analytical models that accurately describe key properties such as porosity, film thickness, and current density distribution in electrochemical systems with complex geometries. Initial studies are devoted to heterogeneous models of nanoporous gold (NPG) and platinum on carbon (Pt/C), highlighting how variations in pore structure impact electrochemical responses. These findings led to the development of improved analytical equations that capture the dynamics of mass transport more effectively. Subsequently, homogeneous models are introduced to simplify the representation of transport by diffusion properties while maintaining accuracy across a range of porosities. A new analytical equation for SECM approach curves was developed, validated through simulations, and shown to be applicable under diverse experimental conditions. The thesis further examines lithium electrodes and SEI evolution using numerical simulations to model the secondary current density distribution under realistic conditions. The results demonstrate how probe positioning and geometry affect the local current density distribution and data interpretation, offering practical guidance for minimizing measurement artefacts in SEI studies. Overall, this work provides valuable tools for optimizing electrode design and contributes to advancing high-performance electrochemical systems.
